pages.text: It was the height of the dry season. The pools had shrunk to cracked mud, and the great river was a long walk away across the plain. A young hunter named Demba was crossing that plain when he heard a groan. In the dust lay a crocodile. His pool had dried up, and he was too weak to reach the river. “Hunter,” he whispered, “have pity. Carry me to the water, or I shall die here.” Demba hesitated. “You are a crocodile. You will eat me.” “How could I harm the one who saves my life?” said the crocodile.

In the dust lay a crocodile.
His pool had dried up, and he was too weak to reach the river.
“Hunter,” he whispered, “have pity.
Carry me to the water, or I shall die here.” Demba hesitated.
“You are a crocodile.
You will eat me.” “How could I harm the one who saves my life?” said the crocodile.
pages.alt: A young hunter with a sack standing over a weak crocodile lying on cracked, dry mud.

pages.text: Demba had a kind heart. He opened his big sack, helped the crocodile to crawl inside, and tied the mouth with a cord. He lifted the sack onto his head and walked all through the heat of the day. At last he reached the river. He untied the cord and let the crocodile slide out at the edge. “The water is too shallow here,” said the crocodile. “Take me a little further in.” Demba waded in up to his knees. “A little further.” Demba waded in up to his waist. Then the crocodile’s jaws closed on his arm.

pages.alt: A hunter wading waist-deep in a river, lowering a crocodile from a sack into the water.

pages.text: “What are you doing?” cried Demba. “I am hungry,” said the crocodile. “I have not eaten for weeks.” “But I saved your life! Is a good deed repaid with a bad one?” “That is the way of the world,” said the crocodile. “Everyone knows it.” “It is not!” said Demba. “Let us ask the first three who come to drink. If they agree with you, eat me.” The crocodile thought about it. He was sure of the answer. “Very well,” he said. But he did not let go of the arm.

pages.text: An old horse came down to the bank, so thin that his ribs showed. Demba called out his question. The horse lifted his head. “For twenty years I carried my master to war and to market,” he said. “When I grew old, he drove me out to feed myself. Yes. A good deed is repaid with a bad one.” He drank and went away. Next came an old cow. “I gave my master milk and calves all my life,” she said. “Now that I am dry, he is waiting to sell me to the butcher. Yes. That is the way of the world.”

pages.text: “You have heard two,” said the crocodile. “Here comes the third.” It was Hare. Demba told the whole story. Hare scratched one long ear. “I am only a small creature and not very clever,” he said. “You say that this great crocodile was carried in that little sack? I cannot believe it.” “It is true,” said the crocodile. “I cannot judge what I cannot picture,” said Hare. “Show me.” The crocodile was annoyed. He let go of Demba’s arm, crawled up the bank, and squeezed back into the sack. “Like this,” he said.

pages.alt: A hare on a river bank pointing at an empty sack while a crocodile crawls out of the water towards it.

pages.text: “And the cord was tied?” asked Hare. “It was,” said the crocodile. “Hunter, tie it as it was.” Demba tied the cord tightly. “Now I can picture it,” said Hare. “And now, hunter, you may decide for yourself how this good deed should be repaid.” Demba carried the sack all the way back to the dry pool and left the crocodile there to wait for the rains. Then he thanked Hare. The storytellers end with two pieces of advice. Be kind, but do not be foolish. And treat well those who have served you, so that the horse and the cow may give a better answer.

activities.question: Why did the crocodile need help?
options: He was caught in a trap
His pool had dried up and he was too weak to reach the river
He had lost his way at night

activities.question: Why did the old horse say that good is repaid with bad?
options: His master drove him out when he grew old, after years of service
He had never done a good deed

activities.question: How did Hare get the crocodile to release Demba?
options: He said he must see the crocodile climb back into the sack to believe the story

activities.question: Apply it: A stranger asks you to carry his heavy bag into a quiet, empty street. Using the tale, what is the wisest response?
options: Refuse to help anyone ever again
Offer help in a safe way, such as in a public place or by calling an adult

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: Demba finds the crocodile dying on the dry plain
He carries the crocodile to the river in a sack
The old horse and the old cow give their answers
Hare tricks the crocodile back into the sack
